tldr: By pre-allocating memory at initialization and switching control modes via lock-free pointer swapping, this work slashes ROS 2 controller switching pauses from hundreds of milliseconds to under 0.1 ms, allowing robots to deploy reflex behaviours and avoid hazards without stopping their tasks.
hero_caption: An overview comparing the conventional approach with the proposed method. On the left, conventional methods completely stop the robot during controller switches or safety hazards. On the right, the proposed framework switches smoothly in under 1 ms, executing reflex behaviours to maintain continuous task execution without interruption.
overview:
Service robots operating in human environments like homes depend on safe physical human-robot interaction (pHRI). These tasks require switching control strategies on the fly—from fast "position control" in free space to gentle "force control" when wiping a table. However, ros2_control, the standard control framework in ROS 2, enforces a "stop-to-switch" rule that halts the robot whenever switching controllers. This process incurs hundreds of milliseconds in communication and processing overhead. It disrupts smooth motion and prevents robots from reacting instantly when hazards like collisions happen.

To solve this, the authors built an enhanced multimode controller framework compatible with ROS 2 that switches controllers in under 1 millisecond. They shifted DDS entity creation and dynamic memory allocation—the main culprits behind latency—entirely into an upfront initialization phase. Inside the 1 kHz (1 ms period) real-time loop, switching boils down to updating a single pointer. Leveraging this sub-millisecond responsiveness, they integrated five reflex behaviours that safely dissipate contact forces and mitigate joint limit violations before the manufacturer's rigid hardware emergency stops engage.

Experiments on a physical Franka Emika Panda manipulator showed controller switching latency plummeted from roughly 210 ms down to 0.01 ms (sub-0.1 ms worst-case), an improvement of over four orders of magnitude. In a continuous three-stage manipulation task (pick-and-place, surface wiping, and sponge return), eliminating stop-to-switch pauses reduced total execution time by about 0.5 s (3.5%) and cut peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold.
contributions: Realization of a real-time architecture that deterministically switches control modes in under 0.1 ms while remaining compatible with the ROS 2 ecosystem
Construction of a 1 kHz reflex engine that mitigates contact forces and joint limits before manufacturer hardware emergency stops trigger, preventing execution interruptions
Elimination of conventional stop-to-switch procedures, enabling smooth, continuous execution of multi-stage manipulation tasks

Physical validation on a Franka Panda manipulator demonstrating a four-orders-of-magnitude reduction in switching delay, safe avoidance during collisions and limit violations, and a threefold reduction in trajectory jerk

sections.heading: Why Can't ROS 2 Robots Switch Controllers Smoothly?
sections.summary: Collaborative robots require context-dependent controller switching and swift collision reactions, but standard ROS 2 control architectures suffer from structural stop-to-switch constraints with substantial delays. To solve this, this paper proposes a reflex engine that switches in under 0.1 ms.
sections.details:
When robots operate in unpredictable human environments like households, unexpected physical contact is inevitable. To prevent severe injury, robots must detect contact instantly and react with minimal latency within high-frequency 1 kHz (1 ms period) torque control loops, as outlined in ISO standards (such as ISO 10218 and ISO 13482).

Household tasks also demand vastly different control objectives across different phases. For example, in table cleaning, the robot needs high-accuracy position/velocity control to move quickly around obstacles, compliant force control to wipe the table with a constant pressing force, and stiff impedance control to stow tools and return to its initial pose. Since no single controller can optimize everything, the robot needs to switch controllers dynamically and instantaneously depending on the situation.

However, current ROS 2 and its standard control framework, ros2_control, have a major structural limitation. Controller state transitions rely on lifecycle node mechanisms, adopting a "stop-to-switch" scheme for safety where the robot must come to a complete halt before switching. This process introduces communication overhead and scheduling jitter, breaking real-time guarantees. As a result, when hazardous events occur, the robot engages a rigid emergency stop, sacrificing smooth collaboration and autonomous task continuity. The authors built their framework to overcome this bottleneck.

Conventional methods incur over 200 ms of stopping and task interruption per switch, whereas the proposed method switches pointers in under 1 ms to inject reflex behaviours, maintaining uninterrupted task execution.

sections.heading: State of the Art and the Hurdles Remaining in Open-Source Middleware
sections.summary: While 1 kHz torque control and collision reflex theories are well established, they previously ran only on proprietary real-time operating systems. In general-purpose middleware like ROS 2, internal communication and switching delays have made it difficult to openly implement reflex behaviours that meet safety standards.
sections.details:
### II-A Advances in High-Frequency Torque Control
In the past, robot control operated at low frequencies like 60 Hz or 120 Hz, which could not capture high-frequency vibrations during collisions. Today, collaborative robots (cobots) like the DLR Lightweight Robot and the Franka Emika Panda can measure and command joint torques at 1 kHz as standard. A 1 kHz control loop allows treating joints as ideal torque sources using the robot's dynamic model (Lagrangian equations), enabling advanced interaction control.

### II-B Classification of Reflex Behaviours and Challenges
Using 1 kHz torque feedback, external contact forces $\mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}}$ can be detected instantaneously via external force observers. Physically, human-robot collisions divide into four phases: pre-collision, collision Phase I (transient), collision Phase II (quasi-static contact), and post-collision. The initial collision Phase I (10–20 ms) is governed by structural inertia, so feedback control cannot suppress peak impact forces. However, subsequent crushing and clamping in Phase II and beyond can be prevented through low-latency reflex behaviours. Reflex behaviours include "task-maintaining" (altering trajectory timing), "task-relaxing" (temporarily deviating from the trajectory), and "task-aborting" (aborting tracking). However, these were previously implemented only in proprietary research frameworks like DLR's aRD/Beasty or ArmarX-RT, and were absent from widely used open-source ecosystems.

### II-C Limitations of Existing Middleware
In ROS 2, node composition allows intra-process communication via shared memory or pointer passing, achieving microsecond-level latency (around 40 $\mu$s). Yet, ros2_control still relies on lifecycle transitions involving service calls and resource reallocations, which block real-time execution threads during controller switches. While transition zones can blend control inputs, blending can be hazardous during active physical contact. Even an existing shared-memory framework (multipanda_ros2) requires roughly 2 ms on average to switch, failing the 1 kHz (1 ms) safety criterion. Developers have faced an all-or-nothing choice between flexible general-purpose middleware and rigid proprietary real-time systems.

sections.heading: How Sub-0.1 ms Switching and the Reflex Engine Were Achieved
sections.summary: By moving all ROS 2 communication entity creation and heap allocations to upfront initialization before the runtime loop, controller switching is reduced to a lock-free pointer swap. Additionally, a reflex state machine monitors joint limits and external forces to intervene before manufacturer emergency stops occur.
sections.details:
### III-A Basic Structure of the Multimode Controller
This method builds upon multipanda_ros2, an open-source framework for multi-robot coordination within a single process. At its core, the Multimode Controller (MC) does not compute torques directly. Instead, it coordinates multiple lightweight control sub-processes called "controllets." Each controllet claims ownership of specific motor resources and computes torque commands $\bm{\tau}_{\text{cmd}}$ tailored to its task. During initialization, the MC grants each controllet direct zero-copy references (via C++ move semantics) to robot states and command vectors, enabling immediate access without data copying.

### III-B Optimization for Sub-0.1 ms Switching
Thorough system tracing of the roughly 2 ms latency in original multipanda_ros2 revealed that ROS 2 communication entities, such as subscribers, were being dynamically instantiated at runtime. Creating DDS (Data Distribution Service) endpoints and registering callbacks triggers dynamic heap allocations, page faults, internal locking, and participant discovery protocols, severely blocking real-time threads.

This is the key breakthrough: the authors shifted all ROS 2 entity instantiations and memory allocations into the non-time-critical initialization phase of the MC. Consequently, the work inside the 1 kHz execution loop was stripped down to a single lock-free pointer swap pointing to the active controllet in memory. With zero context switches, system calls, or DDS overhead, control modes switch deterministically with negligible latency without disturbing the 1 kHz cycle.

### III-C Reflex Engine Design
Within the 1 kHz loop, the engine continuously monitors boundaries to proactively detect hazards:
- Joint position limits ($\mathcal{H}_{\text{pos}}$): a buffer $\bm{\delta}_{q}$ before hardware limits
- Joint velocity limits ($\mathcal{H}_{\text{vel}}$): a buffer $\bm{\delta}_{\dot{q}}$ before maximum velocities
- Joint torque limits ($\mathcal{H}_{\tau}$): a buffer $\bm{\delta}_{\tau}$ before maximum torques
- End-effector force/moment limits ($\mathcal{H}_{f}, \mathcal{H}_{m}$): absolute magnitude of the external wrench $\mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}}$ estimated via pseudo-inverse Jacobian

The state machine consists of four states: NORMAL, REFLEX, WAIT_FOR_RECOVERY, and RECOVERY. When a hazard is detected, it transitions immediately to a reflex behaviour. Five reflex behaviours are available: Stop (holding position), Admittance (yielding to external force), Joint / Cartesian Retraction (repulsive retraction in joint or Cartesian space), and Zero-G (gravity compensation only). After retracting, the user can easily resume the task with a gentle end-effector push gesture (external force $\ge 10$ N).

sections.heading: Three Experimental Scenarios Tested on a Physical Panda
sections.summary: Using a compact AMD Ryzen PC and a physical Franka Panda manipulator, the authors conducted a three-part validation: quantitative measurement of switching delays, verification of reflexes against joint limits and rigid contacts, and performance comparison during a continuous table-cleaning task.
sections.details:
All experiments were conducted using a Franka Robotics 7-DoF Panda manipulator and an ASRock mini-PC (Ryzen 7 7735U, 32 GB RAM) running ROS 2 with a real-time kernel patch.

### IV-A Benchmarking Controller Switching Latency
Three frameworks were compared: standard ros2_control, the original multimode controller, and the proposed enhanced multimode controller. Transitions were triggered 100 times between 5 control behaviours. The delay between the switch request and the moment the new torque command $\bm{\tau}_{\text{cmd}}$ was reflected in the low-level control loop (libfranka) was precisely measured via cross-correlation analysis.

### IV-B Hardware Protection via Reflex Behaviours
Tests evaluated whether the robot safely stops before triggering manufacturer-defined emergency stops:
- Joint position limit test: Driving joints toward hardware limits under stiff impedance control ($K=800$ N/m) with buffer $\bm{\delta}_q=0.2$ rad (10 trials per joint across all 7 axes, 70 trials total).
- Joint velocity limit test: Accelerating joints toward maximum limits using velocity control with buffer $\bm{\delta}_{\dot{q}}=0.1$ rad/s (70 trials total).
- Rigid contact test: Driving the end-effector into a rigid wall under Cartesian impedance control ($K=400$ N/m) at approach velocities of 0.09–0.26 m/s (30 trials total, 15 N external force threshold), triggering a Zero-G (gravity compensation) reflex upon contact.

### IV-C Continuous Multi-Stage Task (Table Cleaning)
A realistic three-stage continuous task was evaluated:
1. Pick-and-place: Clearing an obstacle quickly using velocity control.
2. Surface wiping: Wiping a planar table surface with a constant normal force (10 N) using hybrid force-motion control.
3. Sponge return: Stowing the sponge and returning to the initial configuration under stiff joint impedance control ($K=800$ N/m).
Standard ros2_control and the enhanced multimode controller were each tested over 10 runs, comparing total task completion time and peak end-effector trajectory jerk (rate of change of acceleration).

sections.heading: Delays Cut by Four Orders of Magnitude, Zero Stops on Collision, Smoother Motion
sections.summary: Switching delays plummeted from 210 ms to an average of 0.01 ms (sub-0.1 ms worst case). The robot safely averted contact and limits without triggering hardware stops, and in continuous tasks, it shaved off roughly 0.5 s while slashing jerk by over threefold.
sections.details:
### V-A Controller Switching Latency
Measurements showed standard ros2_control suffered an average switching delay of 210 ms. The original multimode controller averaged 1.8 ms, whereas the proposed enhanced controller achieved an average of 0.01 ms (10 $\mu$s). Even the worst-case delay across 100 trials remained below 0.1 ms, proving high determinism with virtually no jitter—an improvement of over four orders of magnitude.

### V-B Safe Avoidance via Reflex Behaviours
In joint position and velocity limit tests, average stopping distances across all 7 axes were $0.082 \pm 0.003$ rad and $0.080 \pm 0.016$ rad, respectively. Even joint 2, which experiences the highest gravity load, stopped comfortably before reaching hardware limits.
In the 30 rigid wall contact tests, contact force was completely relieved in an average of $0.122 \pm 0.013$ s after exceeding 15 N. In no test did the manufacturer emergency stop (brake lock) engage, keeping the robot continuously operational.

### V-C Continuous Task Execution Performance
In the table cleaning task, the proposed method reduced total completion time by approximately 0.5 s (3.5%) compared to standard ros2_control (from ~13.8 s down to ~13.3 s). While standard ros2_control dropped end-effector velocity to zero at every controller switch, the proposed method smoothly transitioned to the next motion with only the deceleration necessary for direction changes.
Even more strikingly, peak end-effector jerk dropped by more than threefold, from $499.0 \pm 96.9$ m/s$^3$ to $155.4 \pm 40.6$ m/s$^3$, demonstrating a significant reduction in mechanical shock and noticeably smoother motion.

sections.heading: Why Does This Speed Matter? Insights for Practical Deployment
sections.summary: Sub-0.1 ms switching allows reflex behaviours to execute without disturbing the 1 kHz control loop. While initial impact forces cannot be eliminated due to physics, the practical value lies in shedding sustained contact forces and avoiding hard emergency stops.
sections.details:
### VI-A Open-Source Benefits and Control Cycle Alignment
The true significance of sub-0.1 ms switching latency is that controller transitions complete within the slack time of a single cycle in a 1 kHz (1 ms period) safety-critical loop. Because the framework is designed to stay compatible with ros2_control, any existing ros2_control algorithm can be ported as a controllet, instantly bringing these benefits to any ROS 2 robot.

### VI-B Physical Limits of Reflexes and Tuning
Because the experiments use compliant impedance control to soften and stop motion, some overshoot beyond the buffer boundaries occurs. Therefore, buffer margins ($\bm{\delta}_q, \bm{\delta}_{\dot{q}}$) must be tuned appropriately for each application.
Additionally, during rigid contact, transient force peaks exceeding the 15 N threshold were observed. This happens because collision Phase I (first 10–20 ms) is dictated by mechanical stiffness and structural inertia, where feedback control physically cannot intervene. However, sub-0.1 ms reflex switching intervenes immediately in subsequent Phase II (quasi-static contact) to dissipate continuous pressure, successfully preventing sensor saturation and hardware brake locks.

### VI-C Practical Gains in Multi-Stage Tasks
Saving ~0.5 s in a short task with only two switches translates to massive throughput gains in prolonged operations or environments with frequent mode changes. Furthermore, cutting peak jerk by more than threefold reduces mechanical wear on actuators and gearboxes, which is critical for extending hardware lifespan.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook: Towards Non-Stopping Intelligent Robots
sections.summary: This work achieves sub-0.1 ms controller switching and a reflex engine on ROS 2, enabling safe interaction without halting robot motion. Future work will expand task-maintaining reflexes and explore integration with learning-based policies.
sections.details:
This paper introduced a sub-millisecond controller switching framework that enables safe, continuous task execution in ROS 2 without relying on an overly complex monolithic controller. Eliminating runtime overhead via initialization optimizations achieved deterministic sub-0.1 ms switching performance. Using a physical Franka Panda, the authors demonstrated five 1 kHz reflex behaviours and seamless multi-stage task execution across distinct controllers.

Current limitations include reliance on pre-defined reflex behaviours and manual threshold tuning. Future directions include expanding the library of task-maintaining reflexes that mitigate hazards while continuing the task rather than aborting it. Another promising avenue is using this architecture as a safety net for reinforcement learning or learning-based policies, immediately falling back to classical safety controllers when unexpected events occur.

takeaways: Eliminating communication entity creation and dynamic heap allocations from the ROS 2 real-time loop is key to enabling sub-millisecond control switching.
Switching in under 0.1 ms allows injecting compliant reflex behaviours within a 1 kHz cycle before manufacturer hardware emergency stops trigger.
Removing complete stops during mode transitions not only shortens task completion time but also drastically cuts peak jerk and mechanical stress.
Deterministic, ultra-fast reflex systems can be built directly within the open-source ROS 2 ecosystem without proprietary real-time operating systems.
limitations: Transient force peaks during collision Phase I (first 10–20 ms) stem from structural inertia and cannot be suppressed by feedback control regardless of loop speed.
Safety buffer widths and reflex impedance gains are fixed, requiring careful manual tuning based on task objects and robot velocities.
Most implemented reflex behaviours are "task-aborting" and do not yet integrate autonomous trajectory regeneration to smoothly resume tasks after hazard avoidance.
